F1: 8 genotypes were best described by a linear model, 5 by a linear-plateau model, and 1 by a bilinear model, indicating diverse VPD response strategies across the 14 accessions.
Initial slopes ranged from 3.9 to 26.2 mg/m2/s per kPa and intercepts from 5.7 to 44.5 mg/m2/s, reflecting large genotypic variation in both baseline transpiration rate and VPD sensitivity.

Plastic, High WUE genotypes did not uniformly show lower transpiration: PI398617 combined the highest slope (26.2 mg/m2/s per kPa) with the lowest intercept (5.7 mg/m2/s) among all genotypes, a pattern of near-zero baseline transpiration with high VPD sensitivity.
F2: 6 of 14 genotypes (43%) showed a non-linear transpiration response, with VPD breakpoints ranging from 1.62 to 3.17 kPa (mean 2.49 kPa).
4 of the 6 genotypes with a breakpoint were previously classified as Plastic, High WUE (Chamarthi et al. 2022), consistent with the expected limited-transpiration phenotype.

The two earliest breakpoints (1.62 and 1.75 kPa in PI398617 and PI404191) indicate that stomatal restriction can occur before VPD reaches typical midday field values (~2.0-2.5 kPa), potentially conserving water during morning hours.
F3: 4 of 5 Plastic, High WUE genotypes clustered in the Low intercept - High sensitivity quadrant, consistent with lower baseline transpiration and stronger stomatal responsiveness at elevated VPD.
Nonplastic, Low WUE genotypes were distributed across 3 quadrants, indicating within-class heterogeneity not captured by the Chamarthi et al. plasticity classification alone.

PI398617 and PI442012A (both Plastic, High WUE) occupied the most extreme position with intercepts below 7 mg/m2/s and initial slopes above 22 mg/m2/s/kPa, making them the strongest candidates for limited-transpiration trait characterization.
F4: All 9 measured genotypes showed negative stomatal conductance slopes (range: -0.34 to -0.10 mol/m2/s/kPa), confirming universal stomatal closure in response to increasing vapor pressure demand.
Slow wilting genotypes (PI416937 and PI471938) had intermediate slopes (-0.135 and -0.146 mol/m2/s/kPa) and lower intercepts, consistent with the expected limited-transpiration response.

PI603171 (Nonplastic, Low WUE) had the steepest negative slope (-0.34 mol/m2/s/kPa) and highest intercept (1.22 mol/m2/s), indicating paradoxically high baseline conductance relative to its non-plastic classification.
F5: 6 genotypes with plateau or bilinear models showed attenuated or no increase in transpiration above their breakpoint VPD, while the 8 linear-model genotypes continued to increase through 3.5 kPa, demonstrating the functional consequence of the VPD threshold response.

Stomatal conductance declined consistently from VPD 1.5 to 3.5 kPa across all 9 measured genotypes (range: -95 to -72%), with the magnitude of decline reflecting differences in stomatal sensitivity rather than a uniform, species-level response.

The divergence between TR and gsw patterns at 3.5 kPa - rising TR despite declining gsw in several genotypes - suggests that transpiration under high atmospheric demand is increasingly driven by boundary layer conductance and vapor pressure gradient rather than stomatal aperture alone.
